SkyWatcher — 11/30/25, 6:37 AM
I made a comment about John Woo recently that got some minor positive attention
"I actually think that a lot of the motifs of heroic bloodshed don't make sense in a more modern, corporate dystopia than the one of '89, because it's infinitely more cynical and also lacking in the grandeur of his imperial phase. It's kind of hard to do a story about the decay of moral codes in a world where those codes never existed and trying to abide by something resembling them makes you look faintly ridiculous instead of cool. It's why Johnnie To's work is such a clever update of what Woo was doing, because it was made with full awareness of that reality (and why it's sad that he's a Trumper, because he effectively embraced the worst facets of the world his movies seemed to critique) as opposed to emulating lightning in a bottle.

I wonder what modern students of the man's work will end up doing with their interpretations of it. Emulating its themes, even when done well, won't work because the Hong Kong of the 80s and 90s no longer exists and that's a huge part of the context. Emulating his action is more sensible and popular, for good reason, but emulating that without carrying on Woo's themes means that it's probably going to lack in substance. The only thing students of his work can reasonably do is find new angles to interpret his work from and use those to construct something entirely new from the edifices of those masterworks, and that is a singularly difficult endeavor.

I love Woo and his work, but figuring out what to do with it is a struggle because of his singular voice. It's like how comics artists back in the 60s and 70s and were instructed to imitate Jack Kirby and failed because they couldn't truly mimic his singular voice and sensibilities either. 

I think I'm just hoping for the Mike Mignola to his Kirby TBH. Someone inspired by the old master, but able to contextualize it in a very different time and place. "

Hello.
I don't know if you should check out Bullet in the Head, but I will say that it is, bare minimum, Woo's most interesting work by far. It almost feels like his Disco Elysium, a deeply odd, jagged and uncomfortably personal work that acts as a scream of fear, pain and confusion, reflecting a world he saw as increasingly corrupt and hostile while also ultimately acting as a way for Woo to contemplate both his past and his deeply uncertain future.
It's full of jarring tonal shifts, obvious borrowed motifs and dials a number of Woo's stylistic flourishes up to eleven, but none of it could ever be described as weirdness for its own sake.

Basically the protagonist fights a bunch of psychic rock people seemingly hyper-inclined to violence because they can't care for others, except it turns out that not only can they care for other people, they're hyper-inclined for violence because they've been forced into it by the rest of their species.
The psychic rock people are mostly psychologically incapable of doing violence themselves and use these guys to do their dirty work, sending them to die and treating them like dogshit for having the rock person equivalent of a severe neurological disorder.
This leads the protagonist to actually be deeply sympathetic to the people he has to kill, because in his view they're both people considered defective by their society forced into violence with little to no chance of escape.
SkyWatcher — 12/5/25, 5:27 AM
More complexly, the protagonist at one point fights a group of humanoid non-humans who are composed of an odd molecular mix of silicon and carbon, known primarily for having innately longer lifespans than humans (with many living for thousands of years), superhuman physical abilities, an innate psychic connection to the natural world that varies from individual to individual and, based on their own encounters with them, seemingly no ability to care for others, including themselves, or any capacity for remorse. But then things get complicated when the protagonist discovers that not only is that last bit of information is false, but that most of these silicon lifeforms aren't even psychologically capable of direct acts of violence, with the people he's fighting considered mentally defective by the standards of their species for having that capacity and thus being sent out to commit the violence needed for the species to survive and prosper while being ignored and mistreated, with not much effort spent actually bothering to improve their situation. The more significant effort to make that violence needless, while initially seeming noble (and many of the people carrying out this plan do have sincerely noble intentions), is also rooted in disgust towards the members of the species they send to fight.
The protagonist, himself a deeply alienated person with issues connecting to his fellow man, inescapably trapped in a life of violence, feels a kind of deep existential sympathy for the poor bastards trapped in this seemingly unending war for what it turns out is essentially the survival of their species. The silicon people believe that they're incompatible with humanity given their heightened psychic empathy and connection with nature means that it's likely human expansion and violence will wipe them out on top of believing that their innate pacifism makes them more worthy heirs to the planet than humans, but this means that the world they'd forge if they win is also one where humans are doomed. If humans win, the silicon people go extinct, and if the silicon people win, humanity goes extinct. What makes this especially shitty is that the members of both sides actually fighting and dying in the conflict are so alienated from their species that this means nothing to them. Ultimately, they come to suspect that the entire conflict is a pointless dick-measuring contest built entirely on false assumptions. Still, there's nothing any of them individually can do about it. 
As for why they're forced to kill even though their species is ostensibly pacifistic, let me put it like this. The species still eats meat, but most of them are psychologically hardwired to be unable to kill an animal even if they rely on its body for nutrients. These people are exceptions for being able to kill, so they butcher animals and sell their meat, but not only are they disdained by their species for doing something they find distasteful, they're also considered mentally deficient or deviant for even having the capacity to do it in the first place. 
(They "need" meat about as much as humans do, BTW, in that it's recommended for health reasons but not necessary).
(Also they can turn into rocks and live for long periods of time, though they have to stop at some point and they have to consume nutrients in and out of rock form, sort of like hibernation).
The psychic connection with the world around them is why they can't kill animals, people., themselves, really anything. They feel the pain of the animals they kill, so they mostly can't do it. The people who can kill animals are people who can cut off (well, I say cut off, it's more like it's off by default and establishing it is physically and psychologically taxing) or are actively lacking that psychic connection to begin with, hence why they're considered mentally deficient.
That psychic link is also why they haven't gone extinct yet, allowing them to avoid danger and keep safe for long periods of time.
It also acts a convenient tool for mass organisation.
Oh, also, as for how the people who can murder don't just kill them instantly? Well, while I did say they lacked the psychic connections that their species had (or else had them but had them off by default and mostly found that connection unpleasant), I didn't say they were immune to them, or so disconnected that further connection was impossible. It's entirely possible to establish a psychic link with them, albeit a one way link that the person establishing has total control over, effectively acting as a collective safeguard that causes them extreme pain and anguish when they try to attack one of their own. It's also what forces them into a life of violence in the first place, because the people "holding the leash" have all the power and they can't do shit.
There. Any questions?
They're a combination Pillar Men/inverted Rock Humans from JoJo.
Also, on the bit about trying to render the violence of their most marginalized pointless, while there's a huge chunk of the movement that wants them to stop going to war, the most powerful members of it just want these guys to go extinct, damn the consequences, which is why they side with humans and are despised by all silicon lifeform parties as turncoats.

I'm torn on Trigun Stampede
I do like that it's taking liberties with the source to suit the 2020s (like simpler, cuter designs, less twangy guitars and faster pacing), but I don't like any of the liberties taken save for using 3D animation.
It's taken a lot of the edge out, which sucks because part of the appeal of the manga was that it was a dark and gritty romp that starred a light-hearted goof trying his level best to keep his head above water in the dystopian nightmare that is the planet he's on. 
Like Dorohedoro, except where the characters of that manga have long accepted the world in which they live and their happy-go-lucky natures are legit, no one in Trigun accepts the world in which they live and everyone's behaviour is a facade covering overwhelming despair.
SkyWatcher — 1/15/26, 9:48 AM
Trigun was also very heavily influenced by things like V-kei, RPGs, concept artists like Yasushi Nirawasa, Keita Amemiya and Katsuya Terada, 90s action movies like The Matrix, Hard Boiled and Desperado, sci-fi manga by Leiji Matsumoto and Katsuhiro Otomo, and lots and lots of American comics artists popular (and kind of obscure) in the era, like McFarlane, Mike Mignola and Geof Darrow. 
There's a sort of harsh, gaudy maximalism to its aesthetic that works owing to Nightow having a genuinely excellent sense for design, which I don't fully see in Stampede.
